(Her) mother, Tiffany Falden, said her daughter was home on holiday break, and that she was the student government president in her senior year at Dr. Henry A. Wise Jr. High School in Prince George's County, Maryland. "Just loving, caring, a great heart, loves children, loves her family. [She was] just an all-around good girl. Never been in trouble a day in her life," Falden said. Her grandfather, the Rev. Kenneth Thomas Sr., gave her eulogy. Ashlei was Thomas's biggest fan. She called him "Poppi,"; he called her "The Ash." When he got his preacher's license, she made sure everyone knew. She had asked him for a Bible to study with her younger sister. And when she was anxious about taking some tests during her first month or so at Louisiana State University, she called him for encouragement. Thomas stepped to the pulpit. "Ashlei was a special child." He paused. Inhaled. "I loved Ash more than anyone will ever know," Thomas continued, his voice cracking. "I was so proud of her." ... "Everybody that came in contact with Ashlei left differently," he said, his voice rising. "Why? Because she was full of love."

We each can play a role to prevent this from happening to anyone else. If you suspect a woman is the victim of domestic violence, tell someone. Don't leave her alone. If you are in an unsafe relationship, or if you are concerned about a friend or family member who is experiencing domestic violence, you can seek help.
